tips.title: Seven groups, longest first
tips.body: **R**adio, **M**icrowave, **I**nfrared, **V**isible, **U**ltraviolet, **X**-rays, **G**amma. Say it as one phrase and always start from radio, so you never have to work out which end you are at. Wavelength falls and frequency rises as you go along.

tips.title: Metres before anything else
tips.body: If a wavelength arrives in nm, mm or cm, convert it to **metres** before touching $v = f\lambda$. A nanometre is $10^{-9}$ m and a centimetre is $10^{-2}$ m. Almost every lost mark in this topic is a conversion that never happened.

tips.title: Speed is never the answer
tips.body: Any question asking why one type is better for a job, or more dangerous, is never answered by speed: they all travel at the same speed. Look instead at what the wave does at a boundary, whether it is **absorbed**, **transmitted** or **reflected** by that material.

tips.title: Tiny wavelength, huge frequency
tips.body: Their product is fixed at $3 \times 10^8$, so the two always move in opposite directions. If you get a wavelength of $10^{-10}$ m and a frequency that is also tiny, you have multiplied where you should have divided.

steps.title: What the electromagnetic spectrum is
steps.body:
Light is one member of a much larger family. **Electromagnetic waves** are **transverse** waves that **transfer energy from a source to an absorber**.

Three facts carry most of the marks in this topic, and all three are worth learning word for word.

- They are **transverse**: the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer.
- They form a **continuous spectrum**. The groups have names, but there is no gap between them, and no sharp edge where one stops and the next begins.
- **All of them travel at the same speed** through a vacuum or air, about $3 \times 10^8$ m/s. A radio wave and a gamma ray cross a room in exactly the same time.

That last point catches people out. Gamma rays are far more dangerous than radio waves, but not because they travel faster. They do not.

Our eyes detect only **visible light**, which is a very narrow strip of the whole spectrum. Everything else is there whether we can see it or not.

steps.title: The seven groups, in order
steps.body:
Going from **long wavelength to short wavelength**, which is the same as going from **low frequency to high frequency**, the groups are:

**radio · microwave · infrared · visible light · ultraviolet · X-rays · gamma rays**

Visible light itself runs from **red** at the long-wavelength end to **violet** at the short-wavelength end.

Two things to hold on to:

- Wavelength and frequency run in **opposite** directions. As you move right along the list the wavelength gets shorter and the frequency gets higher. That is $v = f\lambda$ at work: the speed is fixed, so one can only rise if the other falls.
- The dangerous end is the **short-wavelength, high-frequency** end. Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays carry the most energy per wave, and they are the three that harm tissue.

An exam question that gives you a wavelength and asks which group it belongs to is really asking whether you know this order.

steps.title: Using v = f λ
steps.body:
Because every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed, one equation connects the whole spectrum.

$$v = f \lambda$$

Wave speed $v$ in m/s, frequency $f$ in hertz (Hz), wavelength $\lambda$ in metres. It is **given on the equation sheet**.

For an electromagnetic wave in air or a vacuum, $v$ is always about $3 \times 10^8$ m/s, so you are really rearranging one equation with one unknown.

steps.title: What each group is used for
steps.body:
The specification names these uses, and questions ask for them directly.

- **radio waves** — television and radio
- **microwaves** — satellite communications, cooking food
- **infrared** — electrical heaters, cooking food, infrared cameras
- **visible light** — fibre optic communications
- **ultraviolet** — energy efficient lamps, sun tanning
- **X-rays and gamma rays** — medical imaging and treatments

At Higher tier you may also be asked **why** a type suits its use. The answer is always about how it interacts with matter.

- Radio waves are used for broadcasting because they **travel long distances and pass through walls**, so an aerial indoors still receives them.
- Microwaves are used for satellite communication because they **pass through the atmosphere** rather than being absorbed or reflected by it.
- Visible light is used in optical fibres because it can be **reflected along the fibre** and carries information quickly.
- X-rays are used for imaging bones because they **pass through flesh but are absorbed by bone**, which is what makes the shadow picture.

steps.title: The dangerous end, and radiation dose
steps.body:
Three groups can harm the body, and the specification is precise about which does what.

- **Ultraviolet** can make skin **age prematurely** and increases the risk of **skin cancer**.
- **X-rays and gamma rays** are **ionising radiation**. They can cause **mutation of genes** and **cancer**.

Notice what is *not* on that list. Radio waves, microwaves, infrared and visible light are not described as ionising, and an answer claiming a mobile phone gives you cancer from its radio waves is not what the specification asks for.

**Radiation dose** measures the **risk of harm** from an exposure, not the amount of radiation as such. It is measured in **sieverts** (Sv), and

$$1000 \text{ millisieverts (mSv)} = 1 \text{ sievert (Sv)}$$

You are **not** required to recall the unit, but you are expected to read dose data and draw a conclusion from it. The effect depends on both the **type** of radiation and the **size of the dose**.

steps.title: Your turn: reading the spectrum
steps.body:
A wave travels through air with a wavelength of **1500 m**.

1. Work out its frequency.
2. Name the group of the electromagnetic spectrum it belongs to.
3. Give one use of that group.
4. Say whether it is described as hazardous in this topic, and why or why not.

Then do the reverse: an X-ray has a wavelength of about $1 \times 10^{-10}$ m. Show that its frequency is about $3 \times 10^{18}$ Hz, and say what that tells you about where it sits in the spectrum.

visuals.alt: A blank table for the two calculations, one starting from a wavelength and one from a frequency

check.prompt: A wave in air has a wavelength of 1500 m. What is its frequency, in Hz?
check.solution: $f = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{1500} = 200\,000$ Hz, which is 200 kHz. A wavelength of over a kilometre puts it firmly in the **radio** group.

steps.title: Going deeper: where the waves come from
steps.body:
This step is **Higher tier**, apart from the last paragraph.

**Radio waves are made by oscillations in an electrical circuit.** An alternating current in an aerial makes charges oscillate, and those oscillating charges produce a radio wave of the **same frequency**.

The reverse also happens. When a radio wave is **absorbed** by an aerial it **induces an alternating current** in the circuit, again with **the same frequency as the wave itself**. That is how a receiver works, and the phrase *the same frequency* is the part that earns the mark.

Across the rest of the spectrum, **changes in atoms and in the nuclei of atoms** generate and absorb electromagnetic waves over a very wide range of frequencies. One case is singled out by the specification: **gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom**.

That is the cleanest way to tell a gamma ray from an X-ray. They overlap in wavelength, so wavelength alone will not separate them. The distinction the specification draws is about **where they come from**: gamma from the nucleus, X-rays from changes in the atom.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Electromagnetic waves are **transverse** and **transfer energy from a source to an absorber**.
- They form a **continuous spectrum**, and **all travel at the same speed** in a vacuum or air, about $3 \times 10^8$ m/s.
- In order of **decreasing wavelength**, which is **increasing frequency**: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
- Visible light runs **red to violet**, and our eyes detect only that narrow strip.
- $v = f\lambda$, given on the equation sheet. Convert the wavelength to **metres** first.
- Uses: radio for television and radio; microwaves for satellite communications and cooking; infrared for heaters, cooking and cameras; visible light for fibre optics; ultraviolet for energy efficient lamps and sun tanning; X-rays and gamma for medical imaging and treatments.
- **Ultraviolet** ages skin and raises the risk of **skin cancer**. **X-rays and gamma rays** are **ionising** and can cause **mutation of genes** and **cancer**.
- **Radiation dose**, in sieverts, measures the **risk of harm**. 1000 mSv = 1 Sv, and you are not required to recall the unit.
- **Higher tier**: radio waves are produced by **oscillations in an electrical circuit**, and when absorbed they **induce an alternating current of the same frequency**.
- **Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus** of an atom, which is what separates them from X-rays.

questions.prompt: Electromagnetic waves transfer energy from a source to what?
questions.solution: Electromagnetic waves **transfer energy from the source of the waves to an absorber**. That is the specification's own wording.

questions.prompt: Which list is in order of increasing frequency?
questions.solution: Frequency rises as wavelength falls, so the order is radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma.

questions.prompt: What type of wave is an electromagnetic wave?
questions.solution: All electromagnetic waves are **transverse**: the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer.

questions.prompt: Which group of the electromagnetic spectrum can our eyes detect?
questions.solution: Our eyes detect only **visible light**, a narrow strip of the whole spectrum.

questions.prompt: Green light has a wavelength of 600 nm. What is this in metres?
questions.solution: A nanometre is $10^{-9}$ m, so $600$ nm $= 600 \times 10^{-9} = 6 \times 10^{-7}$ m. Converting before substituting is what the marks hang on.

questions.prompt: A student says: "Gamma rays are more dangerous than radio waves because they travel faster." Explain what is wrong with this statement and give the correct reason.
questions.solution: The statement is wrong because all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed through a vacuum or air, which is about three hundred million metres per second. A gamma ray and a radio wave cross the same room in the same time, so speed cannot be what makes one more dangerous than the other. What differs is the wavelength and the frequency. Gamma rays sit at the short wavelength and high frequency end of the spectrum, and waves at that end carry much more energy. Gamma rays are ionising, which means they can cause the mutation of genes and lead to cancer, while radio waves are not described as ionising at all.

questions.modelAnswer:
**What is wrong.** All electromagnetic waves travel at the **same speed** through a vacuum or air, about $3 \times 10^8$ m/s. A gamma ray and a radio wave cross a room in the same time, so **speed cannot be the reason**.

**The correct reason.** What differs is the **wavelength and frequency**. Gamma rays are at the short-wavelength, high-frequency end, and carry far more energy per wave. They are **ionising**, so they can cause the **mutation of genes** and **cancer**. Radio waves are not described as ionising.

questions.prompt: Describe the electromagnetic spectrum, and explain why the type of wave used for satellite communications is different from the type used to image a broken bone.
questions.solution: The electromagnetic spectrum is a continuous spectrum of transverse waves that transfer energy from a source to an absorber, and every one of them travels at the same speed through a vacuum or air. Going from long wavelength to short wavelength the groups are radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays, and as the wavelength falls the frequency rises. Microwaves are used for satellite communications because they pass through the atmosphere rather than being absorbed or reflected by it, so a signal can travel up to a satellite and back down again. X-rays are used to image a broken bone because they pass through flesh but are absorbed by bone, so the bone casts a shadow on the detector and shows up on the image. The two jobs need different waves because what matters in each case is how that wavelength interacts with a particular material, not how fast the wave travels, since the speed is the same for both.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The spectrum.** A **continuous** spectrum of **transverse** waves that **transfer energy from a source to an absorber**, all travelling at the **same speed** in a vacuum or air. From long wavelength to short: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays. As the wavelength falls the frequency rises.

**Satellite communications.** **Microwaves**, because they **pass through the atmosphere** instead of being absorbed or reflected by it, so a signal can reach the satellite and return.

**Imaging a bone.** **X-rays**, because they **pass through flesh but are absorbed by bone**, so the bone casts a shadow on the detector.

**Why they differ.** The choice depends on **how that wavelength interacts with a particular material**, not on speed: the speed is the same for both.

questions.prompt: A microwave has a frequency of $1.2 \times 10^{10}$ Hz. The speed of light is $3.0 \times 10^8$ m/s. Calculate its wavelength in metres. Give your answer in standard form.
questions.solution: Rearrange $v = f\lambda$ to $\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8}{1.2 \times 10^{10}}$. Divide the numbers, $3.0 \div 1.2 = 2.5$, and subtract the powers, $10^{8-10} = 10^{-2}$: **2.5 × 10⁻²** m, which is 0.025 m. Typing it as 2.5×10^-2 is exactly what the ×10ⁿ key is for.

examTechnique.body:
Start by working out which of the three things a question wants: the **order** of the spectrum, a **calculation** with $v = f\lambda$, or a **use or hazard**.

For a calculation, convert the wavelength to **metres** first and write the conversion down. Then rearrange, substitute $3 \times 10^8$ for the speed, and give the answer in standard form if it is very large or very small.

For a use, name the group and the application the specification names. For a Higher tier *why* question, say what the wave does when it meets the material: passes through it, is absorbed by it, or is reflected by it.

For a hazard, keep the two statements separate. Ultraviolet ages skin and raises the risk of skin cancer. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and can mutate genes and cause cancer.

And whenever an answer is tempted to explain something by speed, stop. Every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed in a vacuum.
examinerErrors: Saying gamma rays travel faster than radio waves. All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
Substituting a wavelength in nm or cm into v = f λ without converting to metres.
Giving the spectrum in the wrong direction, so radio ends up at the high-frequency end.
Calling radio waves or microwaves ionising. Only X-rays and gamma rays are described that way.
Describing ultraviolet as causing gene mutation, which is the X-ray and gamma statement, rather than skin ageing and skin cancer.
Saying an absorbed radio wave induces a direct current, rather than an alternating current of the same frequency.
Treating radiation dose as the amount of radiation rather than a measure of the risk of harm.
Separating X-rays from gamma rays by wavelength. Their ranges overlap; gamma is defined by coming from the nucleus.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer never reaches for speed as an explanation, because it knows the speed is the same for every electromagnetic wave, and says so explicitly when a question invites the mistake. It converts a wavelength to metres on its own line before substituting, and gives very large or very small answers in standard form. For a use it names the property that matters, saying whether the wave is transmitted, absorbed or reflected by the material in question, rather than asserting that one wave is simply better. It keeps the ultraviolet hazard and the X-ray and gamma hazard distinct, and it separates gamma from X-rays by origin, knowing that their wavelengths overlap.
